quizzes.title: Atoms, Electrons, and the Periodic Table

questions.q: About how many particles are in one mole? [1.2]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.2: One mole is about 6.02 × 10²³ particles.
B is wrong: The exponent is positive; a mole is an enormous number.
C is wrong: A mole is far larger than a thousand.
D is wrong: That is the Coulomb constant, not Avogadro's number.

questions.q: In hydrogen, the drop from level three to level two emits light of about what wavelength? [1.5]
options: About 656 nm, red light, from an energy gap of about 1.9 eV
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.5: A fixed energy gap gives a fixed photon wavelength, λ = hc/ΔE.
A is wrong: That is the drop from level two to level one.
C is wrong: The energy gap is far too large for microwaves.
D is wrong: Hydrogen emits only sharp lines.

questions.q: What does the Pauli exclusion principle imply for an orbital? [1.8]
options: It holds at most eight electrons
It holds any number of electrons with the same spin
It must contain exactly one electron
It holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.8: No two electrons in an atom may share all four quantum numbers.
A is wrong: Eight is the capacity of an s plus p shell, not one orbital.
B is wrong: Same-spin electrons cannot share an orbital.
C is wrong: Orbitals may hold zero, one, or two.

questions.q: What is the electron configuration of sodium, with eleven electrons? [1.9]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.9: Orbitals fill from the lowest energy upward by the aufbau principle.
B is wrong: A p subshell holds at most six electrons.
C is wrong: 3s fills before 3p.
D is wrong: An s subshell holds at most two electrons.

questions.q: How do atomic radius and ionisation energy vary across a period? [1.13]
options: Radius increases and ionisation energy falls
Radius decreases and ionisation energy rises
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.13: Effective nuclear charge rises across a period, pulling valence electrons in more tightly.
A is wrong: That is the trend down a group.
C is wrong: They move in opposite directions.
D is wrong: Both change smoothly across a period.

questions.q: Why does magnesium oxide have a much larger lattice energy than sodium chloride? [2.3]
options: Its ions carry charges of 2+ and 2− and are smaller, so the Coulomb attraction is much stronger
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.3: Attraction grows with the product of ionic charges and falls with distance; MgO's lattice energy is nearly five times that of NaCl.
A is wrong: MgO is an ionic solid.
B is wrong: Smaller ions make the attraction stronger.
D is wrong: Its ions are Mg²⁺ and O²⁻.

questions.q: By VSEPR, what shape and angle do four electron domains with no lone pairs give, as in methane? [2.7]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.7: Electron domains spread as far apart as possible.
A is wrong: Four domains spread further apart in three dimensions.
B is wrong: That is for three domains.
C is wrong: That is for two domains.

questions.q: Why is the H–O–H angle in water smaller than the tetrahedral angle? [2.8]
options: Its two lone pairs take up more room than bonding pairs, squeezing the bonds together
Water has only two electron domains
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.8: Water has four domains, two of them lone pairs, giving a bent shape near 104.5°.
B is wrong: It has two bonds and two lone pairs, four domains.
C is wrong: The cause is lone-pair repulsion.
D is wrong: Water is bent.

questions.q: Why is carbon dioxide non-polar although its C=O bonds are polar? [2.9]
options: Carbon and oxygen have equal electronegativity
It has lone pairs on carbon
The molecule is linear, so the two bond dipoles cancel
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.9: Overall polarity depends on both bond polarity and shape.
A is wrong: Oxygen is more electronegative, so the bonds are polar.
B is wrong: Carbon in CO₂ has no lone pairs.
C is wrong: CO₂ is covalent.

questions.q: What does molecular orbital theory explain about O₂ that simple Lewis structures miss? [2.11]
options: O₂ has two unpaired electrons, so liquid oxygen is attracted to a magnet
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.11: Filling bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals leaves two unpaired electrons.
A is wrong: Its bond order is two.
C is wrong: O₂ is a covalent molecule.
D is wrong: It has a bond order of two.

questions.q: How many atoms does a face-centred cubic unit cell contain? [3.4]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.4: Eight corners × 1/8 + six faces × 1/2 = 1 + 3 = 4.
B is wrong: That is body-centred cubic.
C is wrong: That is simple cubic.
D is wrong: Shared atoms count only in part.

questions.q: Which cubic arrangement has the highest packing efficiency? [3.5]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.5: FCC, like hexagonal close packing, reaches the largest value possible for equal spheres.
A is wrong: Simple cubic is the least efficient.
B is wrong: BCC is between the two.
D is wrong: They differ markedly.

questions.q: What is the coordination number in an FCC metal? [3.6]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.6: Each atom has twelve nearest neighbours in FCC and in hexagonal close packing.
A is wrong: That is simple cubic.
B is wrong: That is BCC.
D is wrong: That is far too few for a close-packed metal.

questions.q: What does Bragg's law state? [3.9]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.9: Waves reflected from successive planes add when the extra path, 2d sin θ, is a whole number of wavelengths.
A is wrong: The extra path is twice d sin θ, and n may be any whole number.
B is wrong: The path difference is proportional to sin θ.
D is wrong: θ is measured from the planes, giving sine.

questions.q: How do metals deform permanently? [3.12]
options: By breaking all the bonds on a plane at once
By the movement of dislocations through the crystal
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.12: Dislocations glide by breaking and remaking only a row of bonds at a time.
A is wrong: That would need far more force than is observed.
B is wrong: Plastic deformation is a slip process.
C is wrong: Boundaries obstruct dislocations; they do not melt.

questions.q: What is the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state? [4.4]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.4: Formation enthalpies are measured relative to the elements in their standard states.
A is wrong: It is defined as zero.
C is wrong: Lattice energy is a different quantity.
D is wrong: It is zero by definition.

questions.q: When is a process at constant temperature and pressure spontaneous? [4.7]
options: When ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.7: Negative ΔG means thermodynamically favoured, though not necessarily fast.
A is wrong: Ice melting is spontaneous though endothermic.
B is wrong: Negative entropy change works against spontaneity.
C is wrong: Positive ΔG means not spontaneous.

questions.q: If ΔH is positive and ΔS positive, when is the process spontaneous? [4.8]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.8: The −TΔS term must outweigh ΔH, which happens above a threshold temperature.
A is wrong: That is for negative ΔH and positive ΔS.
B is wrong: That is for positive ΔH and negative ΔS.
C is wrong: Low temperature favours negative ΔH with negative ΔS.

questions.q: What does ΔG° = −RT ln K imply for a reaction with negative ΔG°? [4.11]
options: K is greater than one, so products are favoured
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.11: At room temperature, each 5.7 kJ/mol change in ΔG° changes K tenfold.
B is wrong: That is for positive ΔG°.
C is wrong: K is always positive.
D is wrong: Thermodynamics says nothing about speed.

questions.q: By Le Chatelier's principle, what happens when a product is removed from an equilibrium mixture? [4.13]
options: The reaction shifts forward to replace it
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.13: The system shifts to partly counteract the disturbance.
A is wrong: Removing product favours the forward reaction.
C is wrong: Concentration changes do not change K.
D is wrong: The equilibrium shifts.

questions.q: How much more hydronium does a solution of pH 3 contain than one of pH 5? [5.3]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.3: Each pH unit is a factor of ten, and two units is a factor of a hundred.
A is wrong: The scale is logarithmic.
B is wrong: Each unit is a factor of ten, not ten units.
D is wrong: Lower pH means more hydronium.

questions.q: What does a buffer contain? [5.5]
options: A weak acid and its conjugate base in comparable amounts
A strong acid and a strong base in equal amounts
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.5: Added acid is consumed by the base and added base by the acid, so pH changes little.
A is wrong: A strong acid cannot absorb added acid.
C is wrong: Water alone has no buffering capacity.
D is wrong: That just gives a neutral salt solution.

questions.q: What is oxidation? [5.7]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.7: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain.
A is wrong: That is reduction.
B is wrong: That is acid–base chemistry.
C is wrong: Oxidation is defined by electron transfer.

questions.q: What is the standard voltage of the Daniell cell, with E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V? [5.10]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.10: E°cell = cathode − anode = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V.
A is wrong: That subtracts the magnitudes instead of the signed potentials.
B is wrong: A spontaneous cell has a positive voltage.
D is wrong: That is not cathode minus anode.

questions.q: What happens to a battery's voltage as Q approaches K, by the Nernst equation? [5.12]
options: It falls to zero, and the battery is flat
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.12: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q, and E = 0 when Q = K.
A is wrong: Products accumulate and the voltage falls.
B is wrong: E° holds only under standard conditions.
D is wrong: The voltage falls to zero at equilibrium.

quizzes.title: Reaction Rates, Diffusion, and Engineering Materials

questions.q: What is the half-life of a first-order reaction with rate constant k? [6.2]
options: ln 2 / k, independent of the starting amount
It grows as the reaction proceeds
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.2: Exponential decay halves in a fixed time, about 0.693/k.
B is wrong: That is the second-order half-life.
C is wrong: Half-life has units of time, inverse to k.
D is wrong: That describes second order.

questions.q: Near room temperature, roughly what does a 10 °C rise do to many reaction rates? [6.5]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.5: The Arrhenius factor e^(−Ea/RT) is very sensitive to temperature.
B is wrong: Rates depend strongly on temperature.
C is wrong: Higher temperature raises rates.
D is wrong: The usual rule of thumb is about a factor of two.

questions.q: What does a catalyst change? [6.6]
options: The activation energy, by providing a different pathway
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.6: It speeds forward and reverse reactions alike and is not consumed.
A is wrong: A catalyst does not change K.
C is wrong: ΔG is unchanged.
D is wrong: Equilibrium composition is unchanged; it is reached faster.

questions.q: If atoms diffuse a certain depth in one hour, how long to diffuse twice as deep? [6.9]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.9: Diffusion distance grows with √(Dt), so doubling depth takes four times as long.
A is wrong: Depth grows with the square root of time.
B is wrong: Deeper diffusion takes longer.
C is wrong: The relation is square, not cube.

questions.q: Why does a semiconductor's conductivity rise with temperature? [6.13]
options: Its band gap is very wide
More electrons are thermally excited across its modest band gap
It has a partly filled band like a metal
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.13: Silicon's gap is about 1.1 eV, small enough for some thermal excitation.
A is wrong: A wide gap is the mark of an insulator.
C is wrong: Metals' conductivity falls with temperature.
D is wrong: The key is carriers crossing the gap.
